title: The Happy Place of Saturday Morning Cartoons
summary: Josh and Chuck reminisce about Saturday morning cartoons, tracing their history from radio-era kids programming and the 1955 Mighty Mouse debut through the 1960s network cartoon blocks, the 1980s toy-based cartoon boom, and the FTC and FCC efforts over children's advertising, including pro-social programming like PSAs, the Children's Television Act of 1990, and the decline of the format (last block on The CW in September 2014). They also discuss cereal ads, nostalgic snacks, and close with a listener email about a flying cockroach.

segments.title: Opening banter and personal Saturday morning memories
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about a Bob Nastanovich encounter and reminisce about their childhood Saturday morning routines, including Thunder the Barbarian and sibling viewing habits.

segments.title: What Saturday morning cartoons were and early history
segments.summary: They describe Saturday morning as a shared cultural ritual with ads aimed at kids. Cartoons had been in movie theaters before TV; Crusader Rabbit (1950) and Mighty Mouse's 1955 CBS debut were early TV milestones.

segments.title: Primetime cartoons move to Saturday and the 1966 cartoon blocks
segments.summary: Shows like The Flintstones and The Jetsons ran in primetime in 1960 before networks consolidated cartoons into Saturday mornings around 1967. Paul Pogue is cited for 1966 as the year all three networks ran cartoon blocks, starting a golden age.

segments.title: Pre-VCR viewing, no choice, and shared culture
segments.summary: Without DVRs or VCRs, kids relied on local newspaper listings and had to watch what networks scheduled. Hosts argue the shared viewing built a common culture, and mention Schoolhouse Rock and the Great Kazoo.

segments.title: Fall lineup ads and the blurring of content and advertising
segments.summary: Networks published annual comic book ads announcing the fall Saturday cartoon lineup. In the 1970s, cartoons became marketing tools, with shows based on existing properties and products like Care Bears and the Smurfs that drove toy sales.
topics: fall TV lineup comic book ads

segments.title: 1980s toy-based cartoons and Reagan-era deregulation
segments.summary: Hosts list 1980s toy-driven cartoons including Pac-Man, Transformers, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Jem, Rambo and Chuck Norris shows, and Strawberry Shortcake and My Little Pony. The cartoons became half-hour commercials in the deregulatory Reagan era.

segments.title: FTC report on sugary food ads and kids' advertising
segments.summary: A late-1970s FTC study found heavy sugary food advertising to kids, with about 95.7 percent of ads for sugary foods in the sampled period. Only four ads were for non-sugary foods. Timer, the cheese character, is mentioned as a counter-message.

segments.title: Cartoon violence and cartoon-versus-ad confusion
segments.summary: Hosts discuss cartoon portrayals of adults as buffoons and the confusion of very young kids between cartoons and commercials, including mini-cartoons in cereal ads. A Simpsons episode about Action Figure Man is referenced.

segments.title: Parent conflict studies and the 1978 FTC staff report
segments.summary: A 1975 National Science Foundation-funded study found Saturday cartoon ads created family conflict. The 1978 FTC staff report recommended banning ads aimed at very young kids and restricting sugar ads for older kids; the dental health concern (tooth decay) was central.

segments.title: Pro-social programming and PSAs
segments.summary: Networks ran PSA cartoons such as Schoolhouse Rock, Cavity Creeps, and Fat Albert, plus a deal in which sugary product ads could continue if balanced by pro-social programming. Quaker Oats' Kenneth representative testified at the FTC hearing, blaming content more than ads.

segments.title: Broadcaster PSAs and the 1980s regulatory retreat
segments.summary: NBC's One to Grow On (1983-1989) featured celebrities giving life advice, and G.I. Joe PSAs covered stranger danger. Under Reagan-era deregulation the FCC did not enforce the recommendations; violent acts per hour in cartoons rose from 18.6 to 26.4 between 1980 and 1990, versus five to six per hour in prime time.

segments.title: Children's Television Act of 1990 and NBC's shift
segments.summary: Congress passed the Children's Television Act of 1990, requiring the FCC to enforce restrictions on children's advertising and educational obligations. NBC moved to older-kid programming such as Saved by the Bell and Mighty Morphin Power Rangers; Pee-wee's Playhouse is mentioned.

segments.title: Decline of Saturday morning cartoons and cable competition
segments.summary: Cable channels, the FCC's jurisdiction limits, the educational-programming E/I label, home gaming, and DVRs eroded the format. NBC exited in 1992, CBS in 1997, and ABC ran cartoons until 2010. The last Saturday cartoon block aired on The CW on September 27, 2014, ending with Yu-Gi-Oh! Zexal.

segments.title: Nostalgic cereal, snacks, and childhood ads
segments.summary: Hosts reminisce about Fruity Pebbles Christmas ad, E.T. peanut butter cereal (Eas and Teas), Lemon Lime Bubble Yum, Hubba Bubba, and honeycomb license plate prizes.

segments.title: Recommendation to watch full vintage broadcast blocks
segments.summary: Josh suggests viewing full three- to four-hour Saturday cartoon blocks with original ads on YouTube.

segments.title: Listener email: cockroach story
segments.summary: A listener named Buck recounts a flying cockroach flying into his mouth on his porch while his three-legged dog Trip was outside. Hosts respond and give the email address.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and the iHeartRadio production credit plays.
